head: Two sea turtles nested on a Southern California beach, the first ever recorded on the U.S. West Coast.
summary: On September 16 and 19, two olive ridley sea turtles came ashore in broad daylight at Seal Beach and Huntington Beach, California, and each dug a nest and laid eggs — the first sea turtle nests ever documented on the U.S. West Coast. NOAA and U.S. Fish and Wildlife staff fenced off the nests, then moved all 204 eggs to climate-controlled incubators at the Aquarium of the Pacific in Long Beach when storm surf threatened to wash them away. If the eggs hatch over the next two months, the hatchlings will be released on the same sand to start their lives as the first sea turtles ever born in California waters.

head: Two stick insects new to science turned up in Australia, one hiding in plain sight for decades.
summary: Researchers writing in Austral Entomology on September 21 described Anchiale mabiensis, whose lidded eggs carry concentric rings unlike any recorded in stick insects, and Anchiale robusta, misidentified for decades. They also reinstated Anchiale albopunctata, mistaken for another species for more than a century, and females of mabiensis reach 6.4 inches. Braxton Jones of the University of Sydney said even among Australia's most photographed insects, species are still escaping recognition.

head: A charred Gallic wall under a Paris hospital may mark the town Caesar besieged.
summary: Archaeologists working in the Hôtel-Dieu courtyard on the Île de la Cité uncovered about 20 metres of a wall of stone and horizontal timbers, carbon-dated to between 200 and 10 BCE. Behind it lay a two-metre platform of sand and gravel, a Gallic spearhead and the remains of a burned wooden building, which fits Caesar's account of the Parisii burning their island town in 52 BCE. France's Ministry of Culture announced the find on September 23, and a cast of the wall will go to a museum because planned hospital works mean the original cannot stay.

head: A gannet's mid-dive torpedo shape won the year's top bird photograph.
summary: UK photographer Henley Spiers won the 2026 Bird Photographer of the Year grand prize for an image of a northern gannet folding into a torpedo shape as it pierced the ocean's surface off Scotland. Judges chose the shot from more than 24,000 entries submitted across eight categories, from owls in flight to a heron tangled in fishing line. Contest director Will Nicholls said every image in the competition represents "a real moment in the wild, earned through patience."

head: Scientists found two snails in Montenegro's mountains with shells that swing shut like doors.
summary: Citizen scientists and researchers working in Durmitor National Park and Komarnica Canyon identified Cochlostoma komarnica and Cochlostoma dobrido, two cone-shelled snails barely six millimeters long that graze algae off limestone rocks. Unlike most land snails, they carry their eyes on the sides of their heads, and a disk on the tail seals the shell shut like a trapdoor when they retreat inside. The team, organized through Taxon Expeditions over eight years of fieldwork, says one species' only known home sits in a canyon threatened by a proposed hydropower dam.

head: An amateur astronomer scouting a campsite found a 390-million-year-old crater instead.
summary: While scanning satellite maps of Quebec's remote Côte-Nord region for a place to camp, Joël Lapointe noticed a strange 25-kilometer ring near Lake Marsal and flagged it to researchers. Fieldwork in 2025 turned up shatter cones confirming a meteorite strike some 390 million years ago, and the structure — now named Uhackatik with the Innu Council of Ekuanitshit — is the largest crater found since Greenland's Hiawatha structure in 2018. Lapointe had only been looking for a quiet spot to pitch a tent.

head: A rare slow loris turned out to be twice as common as scientists thought.
summary: Surveys across 286 kilometers of Guangxi found 98 northern pygmy slow lorises, roughly doubling China's known population of the endangered species. Researchers from Guangxi Normal University recorded the highest concentration, 37 animals, in the county of Longzhou, with most living outside any protected area. The species was only recognized as distinct from its southern cousin in 2023 and had been thought to live almost entirely in Vietnam and Laos.

head: Sperm whales were caught blowing bubbles to keep themselves in place while they rest.
summary: Off Norway's Lofoten Islands, researchers tagged 42 sperm whales and watched 17 of them hang nearly still near the surface for anywhere from a few minutes to three hours, releasing bubbles the entire time. Lead researcher Noémie Freymond of the Université de Neuchâtel found the bubbles counteract the extra buoyancy a resting whale gains as air in its lungs expands on the way up — a mechanism scientists had long suspected but never recorded. The whales drew a different breath before these rests than before a hunting dive, Freymond found, evidence that even a nap is something a sperm whale prepares for.

head: Asian elephants showed they can stop and think before reaching for food.
summary: At Thailand's National Elephant Institute in Lampang, researchers built a clear box holding fruit that elephants could only reach through a side opening, not by grabbing straight at what they could see. Every elephant tested used the trained opening instead of lunging for the visible fruit, and when researchers rotated the box, the animals paused and corrected course rather than reaching for its old position, according to Hunter College's Sydney Hope and CUNY's Joshua Plotnik, writing in PLOS One. It is the first documented evidence of this kind of self-control in elephants, and the team says it could help shape gentler ways for people and elephants to share the same land.

head: Biologists confirmed the first new wild cat species in a century, high in Bolivia's cloud forest.
summary: Biologist Paola Nogales-Ascarrunz photographed an unfamiliar spotted cat in Bolivia's Yungas cloud forest, on the eastern slope of the Andes, and couldn't place it. Geneticist Eduardo Eizirik's team compared genomes from 38 tiger cats across South America and confirmed the animal, now named the tilcayo, split from its relatives some 1.4 million years ago — the first new wild cat species described since 1923. The three-pound tilcayo is known only from the Yungas so far, and researchers suspect the region holds still more cats waiting to be told apart.

head: Three wild dogs set an African distance record hunting for a place to call home.
summary: Three male African wild dogs, nicknamed the Mayukuyuku males, left Zambia's Kafue National Park in mid-2025 and wandered 4,126 kilometers over nine months, the longest movement ever recorded for an African mammal. Matt Becker of the Zambian Carnivore Programme tracked the trio by GPS collar as they passed through the cities of Kitwe and Ndola before settling in a game reserve between South Luangwa and Lower Zambezi National Parks. The trek, roughly half the distance from Cairo to Cape Town, is part of a wider study following 19 wild dog groups as the endangered species searches for new territory and mates across a fragmented landscape.
